strengths: The Schrödinger bridge problem is well studied in the continuous-state diffusion literature, but has, to the best of my knowledge, not yet been applied to the discrete setting. The paper nicely bridges this gap, hence proposing a valuable contribution to the discrete diffusion literature.
The paper looks sound and technically strong.
Empirical results seem to indicate that this approach outperforms previous baselines by a large margin.
Strong performance compared to diffusion bridge model.
This method adapts diffusion Schrodinger bridge matching which opens a new avenue for this task.
The experimental setting for molecular optimization is a very relevant downstream task for the discrete domain, and it builds up some baselines for that task.
The work provides corresponding theoretical guarantees.
weaknesses: The choice of the FCD metric the evaluate the graph structure distributions is surprising, since it is typically used to assess distribution learning from a chemical perspective. Why not use NSPDK for example ?
I’d like to see some error bars on your results.

The method description is quite technical, and might be hard to understand for the average graph machine learning practioner. It could be worth it to include a short tutorial on the Schrödinder Bridge problem to ease the reader understanding.
The paper failed to distinguish its own contributions from existing work and to compare itself with relevant works.

The proposed discrete diffusion Schrödinger bridge matching (DDSBM) highly relies on continuous-time Markov chains (CMTC), but the paper failed to refer to flow matching models [1, 2] which introduce CMTC for discrete data domains.
The paper does not address how its method differs from flow matching in the context of graph data, where node permutations and structural changes are key considerations.

The paper does not discuss the implications of using a continuous-time approach for discrete graph structures, particularly in terms of the transition kernels and their impact on the generated graphs.

This is not the first paper solving the Schrödinger bridge (SB) problem in discrete state spaces; works for discrete SB [3, 4] exist, but the relevance and difference between the proposed method were not discussed.

The paper should clarify how its approach to solving the discrete SB problem differs from existing methods, especially in terms of the specific algorithms used and the assumptions made about the discrete state space.
The paper also needs to address how the proposed method handles the computational challenges associated with discrete SB problems, such as the exponential growth in the number of possible states.
The square brackets around the citation should not appear twice.
The name of section 2.2 'SOLUTION METHOD' needs to be optimized.
The supplementary material also contains the body part of the paper.

The structure section 2/3 is a bit confusing because there should be an introduction to the continuous methods (IPF, IMF) as prior knowledge, then a transition to the method for the discrete domain; currently section 2 starts by discussing the discrete domain and definitions together, making it unclear which parts come from previous work and which from this work.
Insights about the transition from continuous domain to discrete domain are missing.

The results only contain 2 molecule datasets with few supportive ablation experiments; more diverse toy results, other graph types, additional ablations, generation results, or visualizations would make the experiments more complete.
